sentences.text: Dineobellator notohesperus is known from a single species represented by a partial skeleton that displays unique skeletal features, including greater flexion in its hands and feet, tighter grip strength in its hand claws, and increased movement at the tail base compared to other dromaeosaurs.
Quill knobs found on the ulna indicate that Dineobellator was feathered.
This predator measured approximately 2 meters in length and is estimated to have weighed between 18 and 22 kilograms.

A gouge on a right-hand claw suggests an injury caused by a similarly sized theropod, possibly another Dineobellator, while a broken and re-healed rib indicates a previous injury survived by the individual.

The holotype specimen, designated SMP VP-2430, was first recovered in 2008 from the Ojo Alamo Formation by Robert M. Sullivan, Steven E. Jasinski, and James Nikas before the genus was formally named and described in 2020 by Steven E. Jasinski, Robert M. Sullivan, and Peter Dodson.
Dineobellator lived in southern Laramidia, an environment characterized by lush floodplains, wetlands, and riparian gymnosperm forests.
The top predators in Dineobellator's ecosystem were the azhdarchid pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus and the tyrannosaur Tyrannosaurus.
The presence of Dineobellator suggests that dromaeosaurs occupied discrete ecological niches as active predators even alongside large tyrannosaurs.
At least eight types of mammals and seven types of turtles from the formation are inferred to have been common prey items for Dineobellator.
The lack of healing on a claw gouge suggests the injury occurred near death, while a broken and re-healed rib indicates a previous injury survived by the individual.

The classification of Dineobellator is debated; it was initially placed in Velociraptorinae in 2020 but later reexamined in 2022 as a member of Eudromaeosauria outside the Velociraptorinae, though phylogenetic analysis places Dineobellator within the subfamily Velociraptorinae.

Dineobellator lived during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian age) in the Ojo Alamo Formation of New Mexico, United States, approximately 67 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America, specifically in Maastrichtian sediments of the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation in New Mexico, USA, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian epoch.
